title: How many turns bring the four-arm figure back onto itself?
description: A figure with four equal radial arms sits on the board, with ninety degrees marked between neighbouring arms. One arm is coloured red and moved onto each arm in turn, and the turns that fit are written down. Keeko's doubt is that the gap between arms is the only angle of symmetry.
teaching_notes: One idea: each turn that lands the red arm on an arm of the figure is an angle of symmetry, and a full turn always counts. Watch for students who list only the angle between neighbouring arms.

source: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equ
video_script.why: The child lists every angle of symmetry of a figure with four equal radial arms by turning it about its centre.
video_script.substitution: the book's own figure with four radial arms and ninety degrees between neighbouring arms
video_script.anchor: the book's figure with four equal radial arms and a dot at its centre
video_script.wrong_answer: ninety is the only angle of symmetry
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko counts only the angle between neighbouring arms and stops there.
video_script.payoff_line: The figure has four angles of symmetry

final_answer.spoken: four angles of symmetry: ninety, one hundred eighty, two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees

maths_rules: 4 equal radial arms, 90° between neighbouring arms, 4 x 90 = 360
turn by 90°: each arm lands on the next arm, so 90° is an angle of symmetry
the angles of symmetry are 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°, which is 4 angles
a full turn of 360° always brings a figure back, so 360° always counts
video_script.design: One figure with four equal arms and a red arm that moves onto each arm in turn. The list of turns grows beside it. Keeko's doubt is that only the gap between arms counts.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, about a figure with four radial arms.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The angle between neighbouring arms is ninety degrees, marked by dotted lines.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many angles of symmetry does this figure have, and what are they?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the figure with its dot; the words centre of rotation beside the dot; a curved arrow round the dot; the words angle of symmetry beside the arrow

marks.fixed: the dot at the centre lights up and stays fixed
marks.name: the curved arrow and the words angle of symmetry appear

narration: <bookmark mark='fixed'/>When a figure is turned, there is always one fixed point it turns about.
This point is called the centre of rotation.
<bookmark mark='name'/>A turn after which the figure looks exactly the same is called an angle of symmetry.

beats.on_screen: Given: 4 equal radial arms; angle between neighbouring arms = 90°
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the figure has four equal radial arms.
The angle between neighbouring arms is ninety degrees.

beats.on_screen: To find: how many angles of symmetry, and what they are
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many angles of symmetry it has.
We also name each one.

beats.on_screen: turn by 90°: the red arm lands on the next arm, the figure fits

marks.one: the figure turns by 90° and the red arm lands on the next arm
marks.gap: the gap between two arms is outlined

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step one, turn the figure about its centre by ninety degrees.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>That is the gap between neighbouring arms.
Each arm lands on the next arm, so ninety degrees is an angle of symmetry.

beats.on_screen: 90° + 90° = 180°; 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°; the red arm skips one arm, then two arms, and the figure fits each time

marks.two: the red arm skips one arm and then two arms

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, let the red arm skip one arm, and then two arms.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Ninety plus ninety is one hundred eighty degrees, and one more ninety makes two hundred seventy degrees.
The arms are all equal, so the figure fits each time.

beats.on_screen: full turn: 360° always counts; the turns that fit: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°

marks.three: the full turn is added to the list
marks.list: the four turns are listed one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step three, a full turn of three hundred sixty degrees brings any figure back, so it always counts.
<bookmark mark='list'/>The turns that fit are ninety, one hundred eighty, two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The figure has four angles of symmetry.
They are ninety, one hundred eighty, two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the figure
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble from Keeko says 90° only; the red arm skips one arm and the figure fits; the bubble is struck out

marks.skip: the red arm skips one arm and lands on the arm after

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the arms are ninety degrees apart.
Keeko says ninety is the only angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='skip'/>But the red arm can also skip one arm and land on the arm after it.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The arms are all equal, so the figure fits there too, and the doubt is cleared.
